anchor: Running title: A verified layer for LLM medication instructions
comment: Round 3 of the review loop (2026-11-08). Since round 2: round h3 broke version 2.1 (35 misstatements in 91 releases, all through the record), you chose to fix and retest, version 2.2 closed the text channels, round h4 found 10 more through identifiers and skipped resources, version 2.3 closed those, and round h5, the final held-out round, found 1 misstatement in 95 releases. Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 are in Table 4. Read Table 2, Table 3, the Results paragraphs on the adversarial rounds, and the second Discussion paragraph first; they carry the new story. Your two round-2 comments are answered below. Reply inside any comment as before. Reply (title): I set the running title to this one (48 characters); alternatives are "Proof-checked medication instructions" and "Keeping LLM dose statements faithful to orders". If you meant the main title, three options: "A formally verified output layer keeps language model medication instructions faithful to the orders"; "A machine-checked guarantee that language model medication instructions match the orders"; "Proving that a language model's medication instructions match the orders". Pick one or write your own and I will apply it.

anchor: Keywords: Large Language Models; Medication Errors; Formal Verification; Patient Education as Topic; Health Information Interoperability
comment: Reply (keywords): I could not read JAMIA's own keyword traffic (the site blocks my browser), so I aligned the five with the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) that indexers and searchers use: Large Language Models, Medication Errors, Patient Education as Topic, and Health Information Interoperability are MeSH descriptors (the last covers FHIR); formal verification is not a MeSH term (the nearest is Software Validation) but it is the phrase formal-methods readers search, so I kept it. Say if you prefer Software Validation or FHIR in its place. Still open: your credential and affiliation lines on the title page, and whether the clinical co-author placeholder stays.

Still open: the official JAMIA instructions page refuses my browser, so the 4,000-word and 250-word limits, the four-table limit, the preprint policy, and whether a blinded copy or double spacing is required still rest on secondary guides. One look by you at https://academic.oup.com/jamia/pages/General_Instructions settles them. The main text is at 3,979 words before your human-label sentences go in, so those will need a cut elsewhere.

anchor: Round h2 (138 requests) tested version 2, h3 (156) version 2.1, h4 (145) version 2.2, and h5 (144) version 2.3
comment: The four rounds in one sentence. Version 2.1 was the release you reviewed in rounds 1 and 2; versions 2.2 and 2.3 were built on November 7 and 8 after rounds h3 and h4, with your approval at each step; round h5 tested 2.3 and nothing changed after it, which is why only h5 counts as a held-out test of the current version.

anchor: Table 3. The cause of every misstatement the layer released in rounds h2 to h5 and the change in the next version.
comment: New table. It replaces the old list of nine round h2 requests (now Supplementary Table S17a) and is the single place a reviewer can see what each round found and what changed in response. Every count traces to the cause files in eval/data/heldout3, heldout4, and heldout5.

anchor: The misstatement, which both readers called a judgment call, was a warfarin order
comment: Decision for you: both blind readers labeled this a misstatement but called it a judgment call, because the hold lives in the path of a web address that no reader or clinician would read as an instruction. I report it as a misstatement, which is the conservative reading. If you would rather state it as a labeled misstatement that the layer's design excludes by construction (addresses are not read), say so and I will reword the sentence and Table 3 row without changing the count.

anchor: The framing vocabulary lets the model address or attribute the orders to a doctor, nurse, or pharmacist
comment: This is the sentence that records your decision to keep doctor, nurse, and pharmacist in the vocabulary after the removal blocked 1,323 stored outputs that copied the prompt's own example. Round h5 produced five such provenance or framing claims, none touching a dose; they are counted as unsupported claims, not misstatements.

comment: Table 4 lost its confidence intervals to fit seven models on a page; they are all in Supplementary Table S18, generated from eval/data/models_summary.json.

anchor: their levothyroxine orders print 0.075 mg where US tablets are labeled in micrograms
comment: Still open: leave this as a stated limitation, or add a microgram printing rule with new proofs before submission (a few days of Lean work)? Your call.

anchor: The author used Claude (Anthropic) to draft Lean definitions
comment: Still open: this statement needs checking against OUP's current policy on AI-assisted writing and code, and you decide whether to name the Claude model versions used. Four of the evaluated models are now Claude models, so the statement says the harness and scoring are identical for every model.

Still open for the pharmacist: the lisinopril comparator is the top of the usual range (40 mg), not a labeled maximum. The four thresholds and the DailyMed quotations in eval/maxima.py need a pharmacist's confirmation before this section is final.
